hints: Use the cosine addition and subtraction formulae on $\cos(3x+x)$ and $\cos(3x-x)$.
Expand both expressions: the $\sin3x\sin x$ terms have opposite signs.
Add the two expansions, identify the left side as $\cos4x+\cos2x$, and divide by $2$.
walkthrough:
State the compound angle addition and subtraction formulas for cosine:
$$\cos(A + B) = \cos A \cos B - \sin A \sin B$$
$$\cos(A - B) = \cos A \cos B + \sin A \sin B$$

Substitute $A = 3x$ and $B = x$ into both expansion formulas:
$$\cos(3x + x) = \cos 3x \cos x - \sin 3x \sin x$$
$$\cos 4x = \cos 3x \cos x - \sin 3x \sin x \quad (\text{Equation 1})$$
$$\cos(3x - x) = \cos 3x \cos x + \sin 3x \sin x$$
$$\cos 2x = \cos 3x \cos x + \sin 3x \sin x \quad (\text{Equation 2})$$

Add Equation 1 and Equation 2:
$$\cos 4x + \cos 2x = (\cos 3x \cos x - \sin 3x \sin x) + (\cos 3x \cos x + \sin 3x \sin x)$$
$$\cos 4x + \cos 2x = 2\cos 3x \cos x$$

Multiply both sides by $\dfrac{1}{2}$ to obtain the required identity:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos 4x + \cos 2x) \equiv \cos 3x \cos x$$

hints: Use the product-to-sum identity proved in part (i) to replace $\cos3x\cos x$ by $\frac12(\cos4x+\cos2x)$.
Integrate term by term to obtain an exact sine expression before using the limits $-\pi/6$ and $\pi/6$.
Use $\sin(-\theta)=-\sin\theta$ when subtracting the lower-limit value, and simplify exact special-angle values.
walkthrough:
Use the identity established in part (i) to replace the integrand:
$$\int_{-\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{6}\pi} \cos 3x \cos x\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_{-\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{6}\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}(\cos 4x + \cos 2x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{-\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{6}\pi} (\cos 4x + \cos 2x)\,\mathrm{d}x$$

Integrate each cosine term with respect to $x$:
$$\int \cos 4x\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 4x$$
$$\int \cos 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x$$
$$\dfrac{1}{2} \left[ \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 4x + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x \right]_{-\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{6}\pi} = \left[ \dfrac{1}{8}\sin 4x + \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2x \right]_{-\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{6}\pi}$$

Evaluate at the upper limit $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:
$$4\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \implies \sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{3} \implies \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$\text{Upper limit value} = \dfrac{1}{8}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) + \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{16} + \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{16} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{16}$$

Evaluate at the lower limit $x = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ using the odd symmetry of the sine function $\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta$:
$$4\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \implies \sin\left(-\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$2\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} \implies \sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$
$$\text{Lower limit value} = \dfrac{1}{8}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) + \dfrac{1}{4}\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{16} - \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{16} = -\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{16}$$

Subtract the lower limit evaluation from the upper limit evaluation:
$$\int_{-\frac{1}{6}\pi}^{\frac{1}{6}\pi} \cos 3x \cos x\,\mathrm{d}x = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{16} - \left(-\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{16}\right) = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{16} + \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{16} = \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{16} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{8}$$
